newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-Buba's Sievert sees Germany meeting EMU goals.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Buba's Sievert sees Germany meeting EMU goals.

text.p: Bundesbank council member Olaf Sievert said on Thursday he expected Germany to meet the tough deficit goals required for European monetary union, without resorting to breaking the rules.

Sievert said Bonn would be able to use revenues from revaluing the Bundesbank's gold reserves, as is currently under discussion, to reduce both its national debt and budget deficit. This would improve its chances of launching the single European currency in January 1999.

"I am confident that the three percent goal can be reached in a manner which fully complies with the rules," Sievert told a news conference. He was referring to the Maastricht Treaty demand that countries wishing to launch the euro keep their budget deficits at no more than three percent of gross domestic product (GDP).
That goal, along with other, less demanding targets, must be met this year if Germany is to make the EMU grade.

Bonn's controversial plan to revalue Bundesbank reserves, delivering a windfall profit of up to 40 billion marks ($23.6 billion) for ailing state coffers, triggered a wave of charges that the government was planning a one-off accounting fudge.
The Bundesbank currently books its assets at their all-time lowest price, or at the purchase price.

But Sievert, while stressing that one-off measures and accounting tricks did not help the Maastricht project, said it was "more or less unchallenged" that returns from gold revaluation could be used to ease deficits.
Such returns could be classified in the same way as tax returns and extraordinary Bundesbank profits, he said.
But the sale of remaining state-owned shares in Deutsche Telekom AG, also mooted last week, would only affect the debt position, Sievert noted.
Sievert said last week's German tax estimates, which predicted an 18 billion mark shortfall, had shown "how large the budgetary holes which need to be filled will be".
"It will certainly be very difficult to close them in the light of the limited room for manoeuvre, which will be maintained in the coming months," Sievert said.
While he was confident that European economic and monetary union (EMU) would kick off on time, Sievert said he would not speculate on which countries were likely to take part.
Sievert also said he saw no need to change German interest rates and that inflation prospects for the current year were favourable, amid strong competition and a relatively weak economic recovery.
The Bundesbank's steady hand policy since last summer was reasonable, he said.

"Nothing has changed in this regard as far as we are concerned. There is no current leeway for further rate cuts. On the other hand, there is also no reason to consider higher rates in the near future," he said.
Sievert also noted that growth in money supply so far was stronger than had been expected.
M3 growth declined moderately in February and March and dropped unexpectedly sharply in April to 6.7 percent -- close to the Bundesbank's target range of 3.5 to 6.5 percent.
However, he said: "The developments in the first months still say very little about whether the M3 target growth rate can be achieved this year."
That was because M3 had been influenced by the customary volatility of the early months and thus was not as significant as later developments, he said.
